full_judgment: 20. Let me now turn to the next question whether the impugned Rules are violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. From the facts disclosed in this case, it is clear that the Rules are directed to certain problems, made manifest by experience, in the service of the autonomous or semi-autonomous corporations like respondent No. 1. in the years following the liberation war, and in order to sustain the presumption of its constitutionality the court may take into consideration the background of the legislation. The Rules have remedied an anomalous situation where some freedom fighters had already received some benefits as it appears from the Memorandum dated 18th March, 1878 and as it is indicated in Rule 6, and some others who could not be granted similar benefits for want of necessary rules. The Rules have laid down reasonable guidelines for selection or identification of freedom fighters so that certain benefits may be extended uniformly, without picking and choosing, to all employees of the Corporation who come within rule 3. The differentia laid down in this regard are reasonable and they flew from actions, abstentions of sufferings in the service, and for the cause, of the Government of Bangladesh by whom the former employees of the PIAC were absorbed in the employment of the Corporation with a clear provision that their terms and conditions of service might be altered. Conferment of certain benefits on these employees who had participated in the liberation war cannot be objected to on the ground of alleged violation of article 27 or article 29 of the Constitution by the petitioners who were not similarly circumstanced with the freedom fighters.
